title: Idempotency
description: Idempotency is the operational safety principle that lets AI systems retry, replay, and parallelize work without changing the final state more than once.
name: Idempotency
statement: Design every externally visible side effect so that repeating the same operation with the same identity and inputs produces an equivalent final state, even if the operation is replayed, retried, or interleaved with other execution attempts.
intuition: Distributed systems do not preserve your intent; they preserve effects. If a job can be retried, the system must treat the retry as a replay of the same intent, not as a new event with new consequences. Idempotency is therefore a state-management discipline: it moves correctness from “did the call happen once?” to “is the final state equivalent to one successful execution?”

engineering_consequences.title: Retry safety
engineering_consequences.explanation: Retries become operationally acceptable because repeated attempts do not multiply side effects or corrupt state.

engineering_consequences.title: Duplicate tolerance
engineering_consequences.explanation: Duplicate delivery from queues, streams, or RPC clients can be absorbed without inventing new model states or records.

engineering_consequences.title: Checkpoint integrity
engineering_consequences.explanation: Training checkpoints, optimizer state, and artifact writes remain coherent across crashes and restarts when writes are identity-stable and atomic at the right boundary.

engineering_consequences.title: Pipeline determinism
engineering_consequences.explanation: Replayed jobs and backfills converge to the same end state, which makes incident recovery and auditability materially easier.

engineering_consequences.title: Concurrency safety
engineering_consequences.explanation: Concurrent workers can operate on the same logical task if state transitions are guarded by unique identity or conditional updates.

common_violations.violation: Side effects are executed before an idempotency key or deduplication record is durably written.
common_violations.symptoms: Duplicate model artifacts, repeated charges or notifications, and “successful” retries that amplify the original action.
common_violations.why_it_happens: The write path is split across multiple steps without atomic record-and-act semantics.

common_violations.violation: Retries are generated by clients or orchestration layers without a stable operation identity.
common_violations.symptoms: Duplicate rows, duplicate feature updates, and checkpoint versions that drift across attempts.
common_violations.why_it_happens: The system has at-least-once execution but no canonical request identity to collapse repeats.

common_violations.violation: Non-idempotent mutations are hidden inside jobs that are assumed to be “just rerunnable.”
common_violations.symptoms: Reprocessing a failed job changes downstream counts, metrics, or state twice.
common_violations.why_it_happens: Batch and workflow code is written as if failure were impossible, then retried by infrastructure that assumes failure is normal.

common_violations.violation: Checkpoint and artifact writes are append-like when the logical operation is replace-like.
common_violations.symptoms: Stale weights, mixed-version artifacts, partially updated manifests, and inconsistent model rollbacks.
common_violations.why_it_happens: Physical storage semantics are mistaken for logical state semantics.

examples: late-arriving event handling where repeated writes must collapse to one logical result

mental_model:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Logical request identity] --> B[Dedup or conditional state check]
  B --> C[Safe side effect]
  C --> D[Persist final state]
  E[Retry / replay / duplicate delivery] --> B
  B --> F[No-op if already applied]
  D --> G[Equivalent final state]
```
decision_checklist: Does every retried operation carry a stable identity?
Is the final state determined by the request identity and inputs, not by execution count?
Can the side effect be repeated without changing the logical outcome?
Is the deduplication or uniqueness check durable enough to survive crashes?
Are writes atomic at the boundary where logical state changes?
Can concurrent executions converge on the same state without manual intervention?

misconceptions.myth: Idempotency means the system does nothing on repeat calls.
misconceptions.reality: The system may still execute work; the requirement is an equivalent final state, not necessarily zero computation.

misconceptions.myth: Idempotency is only needed for APIs.
misconceptions.reality: It is equally critical in jobs, checkpoints, feature updates, and stream consumers.

misconceptions.myth: Exactly once" delivery solves the problem.
misconceptions.reality: End-to-end correctness still depends on idempotent processing because delivery guarantees do not remove all duplicate or partial execution risks.

misconceptions.myth: A successful retry proves the original action failed.
misconceptions.reality: In distributed systems, a timeout can occur after the side effect has already happened, so retries must be safe by design.

engineering_heuristic: If an operation may be replayed, make the identity durable before the side effect.
historical_origin: The concept is well established in distributed systems and transaction processing, where retryable operations, duplicate message delivery, and partial failures forced architects to distinguish delivery guarantees from effect guarantees. Modern treatments of retries and idempotency in distributed systems emphasize that exactly-once processing semantics are only achievable when the processing step itself is idempotent or made equivalent through deduplication and transactional recording.

benefits: Lower incident blast radius from duplicate execution.
Easier backfills, reprocessing, and workflow replay.
costs: Extra state to track request identity or deduplication windows.
More complex write paths and conditional logic.
Storage and coordination overhead for durable uniqueness checks.
Harder design for operations with naturally non-idempotent effects.

limitations: It is harder to apply to inherently non-repeatable external effects, such as some third-party side effects or irreversible human-visible actions.
It can add significant coordination overhead in ultra-low-latency paths.
It does not remove the need for broader consistency controls such as transaction boundaries, ordering, or reconciliation.
It can be misleading if the logical identity is poorly defined or unstable across retries.
